mainTopic: Activities not to begin close to מנחה, which מנחה is meant, and when an activity counts as begun
overview: The משנה says a person should not start certain activities close to מנחה before he davens: a haircut, the bathhouse, the tannery, a meal, or judging a case. If he already started, he does not stop for תפלה, but he does stop for קריאת שמע. The גמרא first suggests the משנה means close to מנחה קטנה. That would clash with רבי יהושע בן לוי, who forbids even tasting food once מנחה time arrives. So the גמרא says the משנה means מנחה גדולה, and each activity is a long version, like בן אלעשה's elaborate haircut or a big meal. רב אחא בר יעקב offers another approach: even short versions are forbidden, because each one might unexpectedly drag on, for example if the scissors break or he faints in the bathhouse. The גמרא then defines when each activity counts as 'started.' For a meal, רב says it starts with washing hands and רבי חנינא says with loosening the belt, and the two fit different local customs. Finally, אביי applies the belt rule to ערבית, and the גמרא challenges the idea that a required ערבית would make him stop his meal.

steps.title: Activities you may not start close to מנחה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists activities a person may not begin close to מנחה until he has davened.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person may not sit down in front of the barber close to מנחה until he davens. He may not go into the bathhouse, or into the tannery, or start to eat, or start to judge a case.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a list of activities a person should not begin when מנחה time is close, until he davens first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that once a person gets absorbed in one of these activities, he may forget to daven or run out of time. So the משנה tells him not to start them at all until after מנחה.

keyTerms.meaning: Close to the time of מנחה
To sit in judgment, to judge a case

phrases.english: MISHNA
A person may not sit before the barber
close to Mincha, until he prays.
A person may not enter the bathhouse,
and not the tannery,
and not to eat, and not to judge,

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא יֵשֵׁב אָדָם לִפְנֵי הַסַּפָּר סָמוּךְ לַמִּנְחָה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not begin a haircut, bathhouse visit, tannery work, a meal, or a court case close to מנחה before davening.

steps.title: If you already started, you do not stop
steps.stepSummary: Once a person has already started one of these activities, he does not have to stop for תפלה, but he does stop for קריאת שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they already began, they do not stop. People stop to read קריאת שמע, but they do not stop for תפלה.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds what happens if someone already began one of these activities: he may finish, and he only interrupts for קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not starting is one rule; stopping in the middle is a separate, more lenient rule. The משנה is stricter about קריאת שמע, which is a Torah obligation, than about תפלה, so one interrupts for שמע but not for תפלה.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rules: 'don't start' close to מנחה is strict, but 'don't stop once you've started' is lenient. The whole גמרא that follows depends on this 'if they started' clause.

phrases.english: And if they began, they do not stop.
One stops to recite Shema
and one does not stop for prayer.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who already started does not stop for תפלה, but does stop for קריאת שמע.

steps.title: Which מנחה time does the משנה mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which מנחה the משנה means, and rejects the idea of מנחה גדולה because there is still plenty of time left in the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which 'close to מנחה' is meant? If you say close to מנחה גדולה, why shouldn't he do these things? There is still a lot of time left in the day!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what 'close to מנחה' means and tests the first option, מנחה גדולה. It knocks that option down, setting up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מנחה גדולה starts shortly after midday, and there are still hours left to daven. So forbidding a quick haircut or meal then seems too strict, and the גמרא pushes toward a later time.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmudic discussion on the משנה
If you say (introduces an option to be tested)
The early מנחה time, about half an hour after midday

phrases.english: GEMARA
Which 'close to Mincha'?
If you say close to Mincha Gedola,
why not?
There is still much time left in the day!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי סָמוּךְ לַמִּנְחָה אִילֵּימָא לְמִנְחָה גְּדוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the definition of a term in the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'close to מנחה' mean מנחה גדולה or מנחה קטנה?

steps.title: It means close to מנחה קטנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes for now that the משנה means close to מנחה קטנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means close to מנחה קטנה.
steps.whatsHappening: Since מנחה גדולה didn't fit, the גמרא answers that the משנה must be talking about the later time, מנחה קטנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Close to מנחה קטנה the day is running short, so it makes sense to forbid starting long activities. This answer will soon be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: The later מנחה time, about two and a half hours before sunset

phrases.english: Rather, close to Mincha Ketana.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question after rejecting the first option
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה refers to close to מנחה קטנה.

steps.title: Does this contradict רבי יהושע בן לוי?
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה means מנחה קטנה, then someone who started eating need not stop, which seems to contradict רבי יהושע בן לוי, who forbids even tasting anything once מנחה time arrives.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says if they began they do not stop. Shall we say this is a refutation of רבי יהושע בן לוי? For רבי יהושע בן לוי said: once the time of מנחה has arrived, a person may not taste anything before he davens מנחה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of מנחה קטנה by pointing to a conflict with a statement of רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן לוי is understood to be talking about מנחה קטנה, and he forbids even a taste, so surely someone eating must stop. But according to the last step, the משנה says someone who started eating near מנחה קטנה does not stop. The two seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: That he taste anything at all

phrases.english: 'If they began, they do not stop.'

phrases.aramaic: נֵימָא תֶּיהְוֵי תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי,
phrases.english: Shall we say this is a refutation of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi?
For Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Once the time of the Mincha prayer has arrived,
a person is forbidden to taste anything
before he prays the Mincha prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא תֶּיהְוֵי תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of מנחה קטנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the משנה means close to מנחה קטנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the משנה lets someone keep eating near מנחה קטנה, it contradicts רבי יהושע בן לוי, who forbids even tasting once מנחה קטנה arrives.

steps.title: It really means מנחה גדולה, with a very long haircut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back and says the משנה means מנחה גדולה, and it forbids the haircut because it is a long, complicated haircut like that of בן אלעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really it means close to מנחה גדולה, and it is talking about a haircut like בן אלעשה's.
steps.whatsHappening: To avoid the contradiction, the גמרא switches back to מנחה גדולה. It answers the earlier problem ('there is plenty of time') by saying the haircut is an extra-long one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the משנה is about מנחה גדולה and רבי יהושע בן לוי is about מנחה קטנה, so they do not clash. The 'plenty of time' problem is solved because a fancy haircut like בן אלעשה's takes hours and could push past the time for מנחה.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (returning to an earlier option)
A wealthy man known for an elaborate, time-consuming haircut

steps.whyThisMatters: This reading removes the conflict with רבי יהושע בן לוי, which is why later authorities treat his strict rule as applying near מנחה קטנה, while the משנה's case is near מנחה גדולה.

phrases.english: No:
Actually, close to Mincha Gedola,
and with the haircut of ben Elasa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by returning to the option rejected in step 3
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case: the earlier time, but long versions of each activity
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה meant מנחה קטנה, which conflicts with רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means מנחה גדולה, and the activities are extra-long ones, so there is no conflict.

steps.title: The long version of each activity
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains each remaining activity in the משנה as its long, time-consuming version.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Not to the bathhouse' means the whole bathhouse routine. 'Not to the tannery' means a big tannery. 'Not to eat' means a big meal. 'Not to judge' means the start of a court case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the answer by explaining each activity in the משנה as something that takes a long time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item is read as a full, lengthy version: the full bathing routine, a large tanning job, a big feast, and a case from its beginning. That is why it is forbidden to start them even near מנחה גדולה.

keyTerms.meaning: The whole matter, the full routine
The beginning of a court case

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה is about close to מנחה גדולה, and it only forbids starting long versions of these activities. רבי יהושע בן לוי's stricter rule (not even a taste) applies once מנחה קטנה arrives.

phrases.english: 'And not to the bathhouse':
for the whole bathhouse routine.
'And not to the tannery': a large tannery.
'And not to eat': a big meal.
'And not to judge': at the beginning of a case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the answer, applying the 'long version' idea to every item in the משנה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining each case as its lengthy version
steps.terutzMaskana: Each activity in the משנה is a long one, which explains the rule even near מנחה גדולה.

steps.title: Even an ordinary haircut is forbidden, in case the scissors break
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב says the משנה means even a regular haircut. It is forbidden because the scissors might break and cause a long delay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יעקב said: Really, the משנה is talking about our ordinary haircut. Why may he not sit down for it in the first place? It is a rabbinic decree, in case the scissors break.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר יעקב gives a different answer from step 6. He says the משנה forbids even a normal, short haircut close to מנחה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 6, the גמרא said the משנה meant only a long, complicated haircut like בן אלעשה's. רב אחא keeps the time as מנחה גדולה but forbids even a simple haircut. His reason is that something could go wrong, like broken scissors, and the short haircut could turn into a long delay.

keyTerms.meaning: "Really" or "actually." It signals a return to a simpler reading.
In the first place, before starting

steps.confusionAlert: רב אחא does not ask why the haircut is forbidden after it has started. The משנה already says that if he started, he need not stop. His question, "why not in the first place?", asks why a short haircut is forbidden at all before it begins.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a second way of understanding the whole משנה. The rule is not about long activities. It is about short activities that can unexpectedly become long.

phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
Actually, it is about our ordinary haircut,
in the first place, why may he not sit down for it?
It is a decree, in case the scissors break.
phrases.notes: Fixing or replacing the scissors could take a long time.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב אָמַר: לְעוֹלָם בְּתִסְפּוֹרֶת דִּידַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the challenge from step 5, in place of the "long haircut" answer in steps 6-7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the activity is ordinary, and the reason is a protective decree.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה forbids only long, complicated versions of each activity.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a short haircut is forbidden, because a mishap like broken scissors could make it long.

steps.title: The bathhouse and the tannery: even quick visits are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: Entering the bathhouse just to sweat is forbidden, in case he faints. Entering the tannery just to look around is forbidden, in case he sees damage and gets caught up fixing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And not to the bathhouse" means even just to sweat. Why not in the first place? It is a decree, in case he faints. "And not to the tannery" means even just to look. Why not in the first place? Perhaps he will see a loss in his merchandise and become busy with it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא continues with the same approach. He applies it to the bathhouse and the tannery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each activity is the short version: a quick sweat, or a quick look. Each one has a specific risk that could make it long. In the bathhouse he might faint. In the tannery he might see damaged goods and get distracted fixing them.

phrases.english: "And not to the bathhouse" —
means even just to sweat.
In the first place, why not?
It is a decree, in case he faints.
"And not to the tannery" —
means even just to look.
In the first place, why not?
Perhaps he will see a loss in his merchandise
and become preoccupied with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב אחא's approach to the next two activities in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case redefinition plus a protective concern
steps.terutzMaskana: Even quick visits to the bathhouse or tannery are forbidden, because of risks that could cause a long delay.

steps.title: Eating and judging: even a small meal or the end of a trial is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: Even a small meal is forbidden, in case it stretches out. Even finishing a trial is forbidden, in case the judge finds a new reason and reopens the case.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And not to eat" means even a small meal. Why not in the first place? Perhaps he will come to drag it out. "And not to judge" means even just finishing a trial. Why not in the first place? Perhaps he will see a new reason and overturn the ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא finishes applying his approach to the last two activities in the משנה, eating and judging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small meal can easily turn into a long one. Even the last stage of a trial can explode. If the judge notices a new argument, the verdict collapses and the whole case starts over.

keyTerms.meaning: To be drawn out, to extend

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to read the משנה. In the first (steps 6-7), only long activities are forbidden. According to רב אחא בר יעקב (steps 8-10), even short activities are forbidden, because each one could unexpectedly become long.

phrases.english: "And not to eat" —
means even a small meal.
In the first place, why not?
Perhaps he will come to drag it out.
"And not to judgment" —
means even the conclusion of the trial.
In the first place, why not?
Perhaps he will see a new reason
and overturn the ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב אחא's treatment of all the activities in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case redefinition plus a protective concern
steps.terutzMaskana: All the activities are forbidden even in their short forms, because each can stretch out.

steps.title: When does a haircut count as begun?
steps.stepSummary: רב אבין says a haircut has begun once the barber's sheet is placed on the person's knees.
steps.simpleTranslation: From when is it the beginning of a haircut? רב אבין said: From when the barber's sheet is placed on his knees.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the משנה's rule that "if they started, they do not stop." It asks exactly when each activity counts as started, beginning with the haircut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule about not stopping only works if we know the moment an activity begins. For a haircut, the starting point is an early preparation step: putting the sheet over the knees. It is not the first cut.

phrases.english: From when is it the beginning of a haircut?
Rav Avin said:
From when the barber's sheet is placed
on his knees.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: defining the "start" in the משנה's rule that if they started, they need not stop.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact moment a haircut counts as begun.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When the barber's sheet is placed on his knees (רב אבין).

steps.title: When does a bath count as begun?
steps.stepSummary: רב אבין says a bath has begun once the person takes off his outer cloak.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from when is it the beginning of a bath? רב אבין said: From when he removes his cloak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question about the bathhouse. רב אבין answers again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too, the start is a preparation step. Taking off the cloak shows he has really committed to bathing.

keyTerms.meaning: From when he removes or strips off

phrases.english: And from when is it the beginning of a bath?
Rav Avin said:
From when he removes his cloak from himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question, applied to the next activity.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact moment a bath counts as begun.

steps.title: When does tannery work count as begun?
steps.stepSummary: Tannery work has begun once he ties on the work apron between his shoulders.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from when is it the beginning of tannery work? From when he ties the apron between his shoulders.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the tannery. Here the answer is given without naming who said it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tying on the leather work apron marks the start of the work. That is the point where he no longer has to stop for מנחה.

keyTerms.meaning: A tannery, where animal hides are processed
From when he ties the apron between his shoulders

phrases.english: And from when is it the beginning of tannery work?
From when he ties the apron between his shoulders.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question, applied to the tannery.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact moment tannery work counts as begun.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When he ties the apron between his shoulders.

steps.title: When does a meal count as begun? Two opinions
steps.stepSummary: רב says a meal starts when he washes his hands. רבי חנינא says it starts when he loosens his belt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from when is it the beginning of eating? רב said: From when he washes his hands. And רבי חנינא said: From when he loosens his belt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about eating and brings two opinions that look like they disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב says the meal starts with נטילת ידיים, the washing before bread. רבי חנינא says it starts with an earlier step, loosening the belt to get comfortable. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא explains how both can be right.

keyTerms.meaning: From when he washes his hands, meaning נטילת ידיים
From when he loosens his belt

phrases.english: And from when is it the beginning of eating?
Rav said: From when he washes his hands.
And Rabbi Chanina said: From when he loosens his belt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question, but this time there are two opinions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Start of a meal: washing hands (רב), or loosening the belt (רבי חנינא).

steps.title: No real disagreement: different customs in Babylonia and ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's belt rule fits Babylonians, who wore tight belts. רב's hand-washing rule fits people in ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they do not disagree. This one is for us, and that one is for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the disagreement from step 14. Each opinion fits a different place's custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Babylonia people wore their belts tight, so loosening the belt was the real first step of a meal. In ארץ ישראל belts were not tight, so loosening them meant nothing, and the meal started with washing hands. Both rabbis agree on the principle: the meal starts at the first real step toward eating.

keyTerms.meaning: This is for us (Babylonia), and that is for them (ארץ ישראל)

steps.confusionAlert: "For us" refers to Babylonia, where the גמרא was compiled, and it goes with רבי חנינא's belt rule. "For them" refers to ארץ ישראל and goes with רב's hand-washing rule. The order can feel backwards.

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:
This one is for us, and that one is for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reconciles the two opinions in step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב and רבי חנינא disagree about when a meal starts.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each describes the first real step of a meal in his own region.

steps.title: אביי: Babylonian scholars who loosened their belts need not stop for an optional ערבית
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that according to the view that ערבית is optional, we do not bother a Babylonian scholar who loosened his belt. Such a scholar does not have to stop his meal to pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: These Babylonian scholars, according to the one who says ערבית is optional, since he has loosened his belt, we do not trouble him.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי uses the belt rule from step 15 for ערבית. His statement sets up the challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For Babylonians, loosening the belt means the meal has begun. So according to the view that ערבית is רשות (optional), we do not make him stop. The wording suggests that according to the view that ערבית is חובה (required), we would make him stop. The next step attacks exactly that suggestion.

keyTerms.meaning: We trouble him, we make him get up

phrases.english: Abaye said:
These Babylonian scholars,
according to the one who says the evening prayer is optional,
since he has loosened his belt,
we do not trouble him to stop.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the Babylonian belt rule from step 15 to ערבית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the view that ערבית is optional, a Babylonian scholar who loosened his belt is not made to stop his meal.

steps.title: Challenge: even for the required מנחה, a loosened belt means he does not stop
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: would someone who holds ערבית is required really make him stop? Everyone agrees מנחה is required, yet once he loosens his belt he need not stop.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one who says ערבית is required, we do trouble him?! But מנחה is required according to everyone, and we learned that if they started, they do not stop. And רבי חנינא said the start is from when he loosens his belt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges what אביי's words seem to imply, that the result would be different if ערבית is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מנחה is required according to everyone. Even so, our משנה says that once a meal has begun, he need not stop for it, and רבי חנינא says the meal begins with loosening the belt. So a required prayer alone is not a reason to make him stop. Why should a required ערבית be any different?

phrases.english: And according to the one who says it is required, we do trouble him?!
But the afternoon prayer
is required according to everyone,
and we learned: if they started, they do not stop.
And Rabbi Chanina said
that the start is from when he loosens his belt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks what אביי's statement in step 16 seems to imply.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implication that according to the view that ערבית is required, a man who loosened his belt must stop his meal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: מנחה is required by all, yet loosening the belt already counts as "starting," so he need not stop. A required ערבית should therefore be no different.
